title: How to Plan Outfits for the Week (7-Outfit Method)
h1: How to plan outfits for the week: the Sunday 7-outfit method
excerpt: How to plan outfits for the week in one Sunday session: a 7-step routine, a sample mixed week, the 7 shirts and 3 trousers rotation, and backup plans.
tldr: Plan once a week: check each day's dress code and the forecast, start with the hardest day, and choose one complete outfit per day from clean clothes. Repeat pieces with a few days between them, write the plan down, and keep one spare outfit for surprises.
body:
To plan outfits for the week, sit down once (Sunday evening, or whenever your week starts), check what each day holds, and choose one complete outfit per day, shoes included, from clothes that are clean and ready to wear. You don't need seven different looks. A dozen or so pieces that mix well can cover a normal week.

Give it half an hour the first time. It gets quicker once you've saved a few weeks that worked. Below is the routine, a sample mixed week, the "7 shirts, 3 trousers" rotation, and what to do when Wednesday doesn't go to plan.

How to plan outfits for the week: the Sunday routine

1. Write a one-word dress code for each day

Open your calendar and the weather forecast. Next to each day, write what it asks of you in a word or two: office, remote, presentation, gym, dinner, travel, home. That short list is your weekly dress code, and it decides more than your taste does. A Tuesday at home and a Thursday in front of clients need very different clothes.

2. Check what's clean

Plan from what's actually available. If your best shirt is in the wash, either wash it tonight or leave it out of the plan. Anything that needs ironing or dry cleaning goes on the list now, not on Thursday morning.

3. Start with the hardest day

The day with the strictest dress code or the biggest event gets first pick. If Wednesday is a presentation, it gets your best trousers and blazer before anything else is decided. Easy days fill in around it.

4. Pick one anchor piece per day

Choose the piece the outfit hangs on, then add the rest: a top, a bottom, shoes and, if needed, a layer. Grey wool trousers suggest a light blue shirt and loafers; dark jeans and a black knit point towards boots. Decide the shoes now, because shoes are the easiest thing to second-guess at the door.

5. Space out your repeats

Repeating is fine. Wear the navy chinos on Monday and Thursday, not Monday and Tuesday, so the week doesn't feel samey. Shirts and T-shirts that appear twice need a wash in between; jeans, knits and blazers usually don't.

6. Write it down or hang it up

A plan you only hold in your head is gone by Tuesday. Pick one method:

  • a note on your phone with seven lines, one per day
  • a quick photo of each outfit laid on the bed
  • a section of the rail with hangers in day order, shoes underneath
  • a wardrobe app that lets you save outfits from photos of your clothes

7. Add one backup

For each outfit, decide the single swap that fixes a weather change (add a jumper, switch trainers for boots). Then keep one spare outfit that works for almost anything, such as dark jeans, a black knit and black boots. When an invite turns up on Thursday, you already have an answer.

A sample week: work days, a weekend and an evening out

This week uses 14 pieces to cover eight outfits, with Saturday split into a day and an evening. Swap any trousers for a skirt or dress at the same level of formality and the structure still holds.

DayWhat's onOutfit
MondayOfficeNavy chinos, white Oxford shirt, grey crew-neck jumper, brown loafers
TuesdayWorking from homeDark jeans, white T-shirt, olive overshirt, white trainers
WednesdayOffice, presentationCharcoal trousers, light blue shirt, navy blazer, brown loafers
ThursdayOfficeNavy chinos, black fine-knit jumper, white trainers
FridayOffice, then drinksDark jeans, white Oxford shirt, navy blazer, black Chelsea boots
Saturday dayErrands, lunch with friendsStone chinos, white T-shirt, grey jumper, white trainers
Saturday eveningDinner outCharcoal trousers, black fine-knit jumper, black Chelsea boots
SundayHome, family visitStone chinos, light blue shirt, olive overshirt, white trainers

The pieces: four bottoms (navy chinos, charcoal trousers, dark jeans, stone chinos), five tops (white Oxford, light blue shirt, white T-shirt, grey jumper, black knit), two layers (navy blazer, olive overshirt) and three pairs of shoes. Nothing is loud, so almost everything goes with everything. The white Oxford, the light blue shirt and the T-shirt each go through one midweek wash.

Look at how Friday works. The blazer from Wednesday and the shirt from Monday become an after-work outfit just by switching to jeans and boots. That's the whole trick of weekly planning: the same pieces, recombined, with the formal day decided first. An outfit planner app can do the recombining for you once your clothes are in it.

The 7 shirts, 3 trousers rotation

If you'd rather not think about combinations at all, use a fixed rotation: seven tops, three bottoms. You wear a fresh top every day and cycle the bottoms, so each pair gets two or three days a week.

  • Monday: top 1 with trousers A
  • Tuesday: top 2 with trousers B
  • Wednesday: top 3 with trousers C
  • Thursday: top 4 with trousers A
  • Friday: top 5 with trousers B
  • Saturday: top 6 with trousers C
  • Sunday: top 7 with trousers A

It only works if every top goes with every bottom. Choose the three bottoms in quiet colours (navy, grey and denim, or black, beige and denim) and keep the tops to colours that sit well with all three. Seven tops and three bottoms give you 21 possible pairings, so you can change the order without buying anything. Smaller wardrobes run on the same arithmetic: the 3-3-3 rule (three tops, three bottoms, three pairs of shoes) works the same way with nine pieces.

What is the 7 outfit rule?

There's no official version. Most people who say "the 7 outfit rule" or "rule of 7 outfits" mean what this page describes: planning seven outfits in one sitting so each morning's decision is already made.

A separate rule shares the name. The 7-point outfit rule, which spread on TikTok in 2025, scores each piece one or two points and aims for a total of about seven, as Bustle explains. That one is about how busy a single outfit looks, not about the week. It's covered with other named styling rules in the sandwich rule, wrong shoe theory and more.

When plans change mid-week

Swap, don't replan. If Tuesday's outfit feels wrong on Tuesday, wear Thursday's and move Tuesday's to Thursday. You're reordering a list you already made, which takes seconds.

A sudden cold snap or rainy day is what step 7 is for: add the pre-chosen layer or change the shoes. An unexpected dinner gets the spare outfit. And if the whole week falls apart, plan only the next two or three days. Half a plan still beats standing at the wardrobe at 7.40am.

Make it faster every week

Keep the weeks that worked. A photo album or a note called "weeks" means that by the second month you're mostly reusing and adjusting rather than starting from scratch. Note the outfits you didn't enjoy as well; they tell you which pieces to stop planning around.

If you keep running short of combinations, the problem is usually too few pieces that go together, not too few clothes. A capsule wardrobe fixes that by choosing pieces that mix freely.

Planning on a screen also works once your clothes are photographed; digitising your wardrobe takes an evening or two. FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet. You pick an occasion, such as "office" or "dinner out", and it suggests an outfit from clothes you own with a one-line reason, which fits this day-by-day way of planning.

faq.q: How many clothes do I need to plan a week of outfits?
faq.a: Fewer than most people expect. The sample week above covers eight outfits with 14 pieces: four bottoms, five tops, two layers and three pairs of shoes. The key is that the pieces go together, so most tops work with most bottoms. A fixed rotation of seven tops and three bottoms also covers a week, as long as the bottoms are in quiet colours.

The 7 outfit rule usually means planning seven complete outfits in one sitting, often on Sunday, so each morning's choice is already made. It isn't an official rule and has no single creator. It's different from the 7-point outfit rule, a 2025 TikTok idea that scores each piece of a single outfit one or two points and aims for a total of about seven.

faq.q: Does a 7 shirts, 3 pants rotation work?
faq.a: Yes, if every shirt goes with every pair of trousers. Pick the three bottoms in quiet colours, such as navy, grey and denim, and keep the shirts to colours that suit all three. Wear a fresh shirt each day and cycle the trousers, so each pair is worn two or three times a week. That gives 21 possible pairings from ten pieces.

faq.q: Is it better to plan outfits the night before or for the whole week?
faq.a: Planning the whole week saves more effort, because you make all the choices in one calm session and can space out repeats and laundry. The night before is a good fallback when your week is unpredictable. A good middle ground is to plan all seven days on Sunday, then glance at tomorrow's outfit each evening and swap days if the forecast or plans have changed.

faq.q: What do I do if the weather changes after I've planned my outfits?
faq.a: Decide one swap per outfit while you plan, so the fix is ready before the weather turns. That might be adding a jumper, switching trainers for boots, or moving a warm outfit to the cold day and a light one to the warm day. Check the forecast again midweek, because a Sunday forecast for Friday can change.
